Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Predictive Surveillance for Andes Virus Transmission in the Americas
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak linked to the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limitations in conventional, case-based surveillance for zoonotic threats with potential person-to-person transmission. In the present opinion and analysis article, the authors argue that predictive surveillance, supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, can strengthen preparedness for hantavirus transmission in the Americas. Current evidence suggests that selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent-related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs. However, implementation requires more than technical capacity. It depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent model governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer to avoid widening inequities between health systems. Predictive surveillance should complement conventional surveillance by supporting risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public health action in areas where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.
papers.journal: The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

analysis.background: The 2026 Andes virus outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limitations of conventional, case‑based surveillance for zoonotic threats with potential person‑to‑person transmission.
analysis.methods: The article is an opinion and analysis piece proposing predictive surveillance supported by artificial intelligence, ecological modeling, and the One Health approach, rather than reporting original data collection.
analysis.results: Selected models that incorporate epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent‑related variables may provide an anticipatory window of 2 to 12 months, depending on context and data inputs.
analysis.contribution: Predictive surveillance is suggested to complement conventional surveillance by improving risk communication, rodent monitoring, laboratory preparedness, and targeted public‑health actions where ecological and epidemiological signals converge.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The 2026 Andes virus outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise ship exposed limits of case‑based surveillance for zoonotic threats with possible person‑to‑person spread. Methods: This opinion and analysis article proposes predictive surveillance using AI, ecological modeling, and One Health, without original data collection. Results: Models integrating epidemiological, climatic, environmental, and rodent variables may give a 2‑12‑month anticipatory window, depending on context. Contribution: Predictive surveillance can complement conventional systems by enhancing risk communication, rodent monitoring, lab readiness, and targeted public‑health actions where signals converge. Limitations: Success depends on interoperable multisectoral data, transparent governance, local validation, sustainable financing, and technology transfer, and the paper provides only abstract‑level evidence.

analysis_zh.results: 结合流行病学、气候、环境及鼠类相关变量的特定模型,可根据情境和数据输入提供 2 至 12 个月的预警窗口。
analysis_zh.contribution: 建议通过提升风险沟通、鼠类监测、实验室准备以及在生态与流行病学信号交汇处的针对性公共卫生行动,使预测监测补充传统监测。
analysis_zh.limitations: 实施需具备可互操作的多部门数据、透明的模型治理、本地验证、可持续融资以及技术转移;证据仅限于摘要。

papers.title: The 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak: a renewed call for global zoonotic preparedness
papers.abstract: The 2026 cluster of Andes virus (ANDV) infection linked to the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius resulted in 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable), including three deaths, and required the monitoring of more than 650 contacts across more than 30 countries and territories before the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026. Available evidence suggests a single land-based zoonotic exposure before embarkation, followed by limited person-to-person transmission on board. Although WHO assessed the global risk as low throughout, the event exposed recurring weaknesses in zoonotic preparedness, including delayed clinical recognition in a remote setting, maritime outbreak protocols oriented toward other pathogens, and the burden of multinational contact tracing for an infection with an incubation period of up to 6 weeks. This editorial examines these lessons in light of earlier ANDV outbreaks and argues for closer integration of One Health surveillance, maritime health security, and the International Health Regulations in preparing for rare but high-consequence zoonoses.
papers.journal: International Journal of Surgery: Global Health

papers.title: Case Report: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Seoul orthohantavirus mimicking severe acute pancreatitis: dynamic imaging evolution and pathogen confirmation by mNGS
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation A 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology. Conclusion Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

KEYWORDS acute pancreatitis, case report, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, Seoul orthohantavirus Introduction Case presentation and clinical data A 33-year-old man presented with one week of recurrent fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He had no history of gallstones, hypertriglyceridemia, alcohol abuse, or other recognized risk factors for acute pancreatitis. Although viral gastroenteritis could explain fever, vomiting and watery diarrhea, the presence of epigastric tenderness on TYPE Case Report PUBLISHED 28 October 2026 DOI 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 01 frontiersin.org physical examination together with marked peripancreatic- perirenal exudates identified on initial abdominal CT raised strong clinical suspicion for severe acute pancreatitis. Initial non-contrast abdominal CT showed peripancreatic and perirenal haziness, renal fascial thickening, and small-volume abdominopelvic effusion with mild pancreatic swelling, findings highly suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis (Figure 1). Initial supportive measures for suspected acute pancreatitis were implemented, including intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, octreotide infusion, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, and volume resuscitation. Of note, severe thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 109/L) was already documented on admission rather than developing during hospitalization. However, the patient demonstrated progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without biochemical elevation of pancreatic enzymes. Two abdominal CT examinations were performed: a non- contrast CT on hospital day 1 (admission), followed by contrast- enhanced abdominal CT on hospital day 2. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed progressive retroperitoneal exudation accompanied by newly developed bilateral pleural effusion and splenomegaly. Routine work-up for undifferentiated fever was sent before mNGS testing, including bacterial blood cultures, stool culture, and a respiratory-borne viral screening panel, all of which returned negative results. Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) laboratory screening was not performed because clinical suspicion for TMA was low: the patient lacked schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, had no severe neurologic manifestations, and mNGS rapidly identified Seoul orthohantavirus as the causative pathogen. Whole-blood mNGS detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus (HBV) and no bacterial or fungal pathogens. Hepatoprotective therapy consisted of intravenous reduced glutathione and magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate. Due to persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and unstable clinical status precluding oral feeding, the patient was kept nil per os (NPO) at admission, not as a standard mandatory intervention for suspected acute pancreatitis. Enteral nutrition was gradually initiated once abdominal symptoms improved. After supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, albumin supplementation, hepatoprotective therapy, and electrolyte correction, the patient recovered fully; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology (Figure 2). Laboratory and imaging findings Initial laboratory investigations showed a mixed acid-base disturbance, characterized by respiratory alkalosis with normal anion-gap (AnGap 2-10 mmol/L),hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and liver function injury. The most striking abnormality was profound thrombocytopenia (29 × 109/L); urinalysis revealed hematuria and proteinuria. Table 2 was revised to add serum amylase, lipase, serum triglyceride, serum urea, serum creatinine, sodium, potassium, hemoglobin values. Reticulocyte count was not tested in clinical practice; hemoglobin levels over serial time-points are presented to evaluate for bone-marrow suppression. Urine sediment examination did not demonstrate granular or hyaline casts. Serial urine output was prospectively recorded as part of intensive care monitoring; overall urine output remained adequate throughout hospitalization without anuria or oliguric renal failure. Mild anemia was observed (minimum hemoglobin 127 g/L). Serial changes in leukocytes, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages, transaminases, platelets, albumin, and coagulation parameters are summarized in Table 2. The dynamic clinical, laboratory, imaging, and management course across hospitalization is summarized in the diagnostic timeline (Table 1). Hospital course and management The initial working diagnosis was suspected severe acute pancreatitis, and management comprised nil-per-os status due to patient intolerance of oral intake, octreotide infusion, a proton- pump inhibitor, empirical antimicrobial therapy, and fluid resuscitation. When the severe thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction could not be explained by primary pancreatitis, HFRS was considered. On hospital day 3, whole-blood mNGS returned high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, confirming the diagnosis. Treatment was adjusted to include intravenous immunoglobulin, human albumin, hepatoprotective therapy, and electrolyte correction. Abdominal pain resolved, and platelet count, liver, and renal parameters gradually normalized. The patient was discharged on hospital day 11 in good clinical condition, with outpatient follow-up scheduled for monitoring of liver function and HBV. Acute pancreatitis is a recognized but rare complication of HFRS (2, 6), and its distinction from hantavirus-induced pancreatic involvement is notoriously difficult because of overlapping clinical and imaging features (9). The present case further illustrates that peripancreatic exudation and retroperitoneal fluid —hallmark findings of severe acute pancreatitis—can also result from the profound systemic capillary leakage and retroperitoneal edema characteristic of hantavirus infection (4, 5). In this context, marked thrombocytopenia, renal impairment with hematuria and proteinuria, and the absence of typical pancreatitis risk factors constituted pivotal clues that prompted consideration of an alternative etiology (9). Moreover, the normal pancreatic enzyme levels observed here demonstrate that Abbreviations HFRS, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; AP, acute pancreatitis; SAP, severe acute pancreatitis; CT, computed tomography; mNGS, metagenomic next-generation sequencing; HBV, hepatitis B virus; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; IVIG, intravenous immunoglobulin; PLT, platelet count; DIC, disseminated intravascular coagulation. Liu and Song 10.3389/fmed.2026.1995402 Frontiers in Medicine 02 frontiersin.org biochemical markers alone cannot reliably exclude HFRS in suspected pancreatitis (10). It should be acknowledged that severe acute pancreatitis itself may produce thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction secondary to systemic inflammation. However, several features argued against primary acute pancreatitis in this patient: thrombocytopenia was already present at initial presentation as a critical-value finding before any expected inflammatory peak of pancreatitis; renal injury was accompanied by prominent urinary findings (hematuria and proteinuria) typical for hantavirus-mediated tubular injury rather than purely pre-renal renal impairment secondary to pancreatitis-related hypovolemia; and serum amylase/lipase remained within normal reference ranges throughout admission despite extensive peripancreatic exudates on CT imaging. (A, C) Non-contrast abdominal CT acquired on hospital day 1 (admission). White arrows indicate the pancreas, peripancreatic fat- stranding inflammatory exudates, and thickened bilateral prerenal fascia with perirenal exudates. These radiological features initially raised high clinical suspicion for severe acute pancreatitis. (B, D) Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT acquired on hospital day 2. Compared with hospital day 1 non-contrast CT, retroperitoneal, peripancreatic and perirenal exudates are obviously progressive. After contrast administration, the pancreatic parenchyma shows no definite necrosis or large-scale parenchymal destruction. FIGURE 2 Pre-discharge abdominal ultrasound obtained on hospital day 12 (at discharge). (A) Color-Doppler ultrasound view of upper abdomen. (B) Grayscale two-dimensional ultrasound image. White arrows mark the pancreatic gland. The pancreas presents normal parenchymal echotexture, without swelling, enlargement or surrounding fluid-collection, confirming complete resolution of previous retro-peritoneal inflammatory exudative lesions. analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome; atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis.
analysis.methods: A single‑patient case report of a 33‑year‑old man admitted to a Guangzhou, China hospital describes clinical assessment, serial non‑contrast and contrast‑enhanced CT imaging, and whole‑blood metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) for pathogen detection.
analysis.results: The patient exhibited profound thrombocytopenia (nadir 29 × 10⁹/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, proteinuria, mild pancreatic parenchymal changes despite extensive peripancreatic/retroperitoneal exudate and new bilateral pleural effusion; mNGS identified high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus (with concurrent hepatitis B virus), and supportive care led to full recovery with normal pancreatic ultrasound before discharge.
analysis.contribution: The case demonstrates that Seoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically, highlights disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and preserved pancreas as diagnostic clues, and shows that mNGS enables rapid definitive pathogen confirmation to guide appropriate management.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a zoonotic orthohantavirus disease that can mimic acute pancreatitis. Methods: A case report of a 33‑year‑old man in Guangzhou, China used clinical data, serial CT scans, and whole‑blood mNGS. Results: The patient had severe thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, extensive retroperitoneal exudate, and mNGS detected high‑copy Seoul orthohantavirus; he recovered fully with normal pancreatic imaging. Contribution: Highlights Seoul orthohantavirus as a pancreatitis mimic, identifies key diagnostic clues, and shows mNGS utility for rapid diagnosis. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 病例报告:由首尔 正汉坦病毒 引起的 肾综合征出血热,模拟重症急性胰腺炎:动态影像演变及通过mNGS确认病原

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种由正汉坦病毒引起的动物源性疾病,特征为发热、血小板减少、肾功能受损和毛细血管漏综合征;非典型表现可与急性胰腺炎极为相似。
analysis_zh.methods: 本报告为一例33岁男性患者的单例病例,入院于中国广州某医院,内容包括临床评估、连续的非增强及增强CT扫描,以及全血宏基因组下一代测序(mNGS)用于病原体检测。
analysis_zh.results: 患者出现显著血小板减少(最低值 29 × 109/L)、进行性肾功能受损、血尿、蛋白尿,尽管有广泛的胰周/后腹膜渗出及新发双侧胸腔积液,胰腺实质改变仅轻度;mNGS 检测到高拷贝数首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒(伴有乙型肝炎病毒感染),经支持治疗后患者完全恢复,出院前胰腺超声显示正常。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该病例表明首尔病毒 正汉坦病毒 感染在临床和影像学上可高度模拟重症急性胰腺炎,强调血小板显著下降、肾脏受累及胰腺保持完整是诊断线索,并显示 mNGS 能快速确证病原体,为合理治疗提供依据。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: A Case Report of Hantavirus Capillary Leak Syndrome in the Southwestern United States.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Early symptoms are nonspecific, but the disease can rapidly progress to severe respiratory compromise and shock due to profound capillary leak. We report the case of a previously healthy 20-year-old man who initially presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and progressive weakness after occupational exposure on a ranch in southwestern Arizona. He quickly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), septic shock, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The initial infectious workup was negative. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure requiring intubation and vasopressor support. Computed tomography of his chest showed pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions despite aggressive diuresis, requiring bilateral chest tubes. He gradually improved with supportive care, was successfully extubated, weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with outpatient rehabilitation. His diagnosis was later confirmed with a serum ELISA test which was positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of HCPS, particularly when gastrointestinal symptoms predominate early in the illness. In endemic areas with rodent exposure history, hemoconcentration and thrombocytopenia, along with signs of volume overload and rapidly progressive acute respiratory failure, should raise suspicion for hantavirus infection. Identification and supportive care are the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient did not require ECMO, transfer to an ECMO center may be beneficial to support recovery during the cardiopulmonary phase, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control.

Early symptoms are nonspecific, but the disease can rapidly progress to severe respiratory compromise and shock due to profound capillary leak. He quickly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), septic shock, and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The initial infectious workup was negative. His clinical course was complicated by respiratory failure requiring intubation and vasopressor support. Computed tomography of his chest showed pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions despite aggressive diuresis, requiring bilateral chest tubes. He gradually improved with supportive care, was successfully extubated, weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with outpatient rehabilitation. His diagnosis was later confirmed with a serum ELISA test which was positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of HCPS, particularly when gastrointestinal symptoms predominate early in the illness. Identification and supportive care are the mainstay of treatment. Although this patient did not require ECMO, transfer to an ECMO center may be beneficial to support recovery during the cardiopulmonary phase, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control. 1. Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped single‐stranded RNA viruses that can cause zoonotic diseases in humans, including the two most common, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). HFRS is caused by Old World orthohantaviruses and is seen in Asia and Europe. Whereas, HCPS was first identified in the southwestern United States in the early 1990s and is caused by New World hantaviruses. The primary route of transmission is inhalation of aerosolized particles from the urine, feces, or saliva of infected rodents. Although HCPS is rare with an annual incidence of 0.04 to 0.19 cases/million persons, it is associated with a high mortality rate ranging from 30% to 50% and poses a diagnostic challenge due to its nonspecific prodromal symptoms. The disease typically progresses from a febrile phase to a rapidly deteriorating cardiopulmonary phase characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, hypotension, and shock resulting from widespread capillary leak. Clinical diagnosis often relies on a combination of epidemiological context, laboratory abnormalities such as thrombocytopenia and elevated hematocrit, and a high index of suspicion, particularly in endemic regions. We present a case of severe HCPS in a previously healthy young man who developed profound capillary leak syndrome with respiratory failure and shock. This case emphasizes the diagnostic importance of gastrointestinal‐predominant prodromal symptoms, early risk stratification, and timely escalation of supportive care. Per institutional policy, this single‐patient case report did not require formal Institutional Review Board approval. No written consent has been obtained from the patients as there is no patient identifiable data included in this case report. 2. Case Presentation A 20‐year‐old man with no known medical history presented to an outside hospital with over six days of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and generalized weakness. He had recently returned from a vacation in Mexico, where he was evaluated at an urgent care center for similar symptoms and was treated symptomatically with intravenous fluids and antiemetics. Upon his return to southwestern Arizona, where he worked on a ranch, he sought further evaluation in the emergency department due to persistent symptoms. He was febrile but hemodynamically stable on presentation. Laboratory results were notable for leukocytosis with neutrophilia (white cell count 38,100 cells/μL), bandemia (10.4%), hemoconcentration (hemoglobin 20.3 g/dL, hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/μL), lactic acidosis (4.8 mmol/L), and elevated procalcitonin (2.43 ng/mL). Chest CT (Figure 1A) revealed patchy parenchymal opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema, predominant right middle lobe opacities, which may suggest superimposed infection/aspiration, and small bilateral pleural effusions. Subsequently, he became progressively hypoxic and hypotensive, requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. Patient samples were pan‐cultured, and broad‐spectrum antibiotics were started. Chest CT on presentation (A) showing patchy parenchymal opacities suggestive of pulmonary edema, predominant right middle lobe opacities which may suggest superimposed infection/aspiration, and small bilateral pleural effusions; and three days later (B) showing worsening pulmonary edema and large bilateral pleural effusions suggestive of capillary leak, leading to the placement of bilateral chest tubes. The patient was subsequently transferred to our center for a higher level of care and evaluation for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). He was maintained on lung‐protective ventilation (tidal volume 5.6 mL/kg, PEEP 12, and FiO2 70%–100%). Empiric antibiotics (piperacillin‐tazobactam, vancomycin, and doxycycline), stress‐dose steroids, and vasopressor support (norepinephrine 11 mcg/min, vasopressin 0.03 U/min) were continued. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal left and right heart function with a small pericardial effusion. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures showed no microbial growth. Respiratory viral panels, bacterial cultures, and fungal serologies were negative. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for hematologic malignancies. On Day 3, a repeat chest CT showed worsening pulmonary edema, patchy peribronchovascular ground‐glass opacities that may represent alveolar edema, interlobular septal thickening, and large bilateral pleural effusions with adjacent atelectasis (Figure 1B); diuretics were started to maintain a net negative fluid balance (at least–1L every day). Bilateral chest tubes were placed, draining 1L of serous fluid each, and pleural fluid studies revealed a cell count of 129 (45% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 30% macrophages), a pleural fluid protein level of 2.5 g/dL (serum protein 5.3 g/dL), and a pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 301 U/L (serum LDH 648 U/L, upper limit of normal 243 U/L). His B‐type natriuretic peptide was elevated (527.8 pg/mL). Abdominal CT also showed signs of volume overload with small‐volume ascites, pelvic free fluid, mesenteric edema, and diffuse anasarca; diuresis continued. He was gradually weaned off vasopressors, and ventilator parameters including FiO2 and PEEP gradually decreased. He was successfully extubated to a high‐flow nasal cannula on Day 5, and antibiotics were discontinued. His clinical status and laboratory abnormalities gradually improved (Figures 2 and 3), and his right and left chest tubes were removed on Days 8 and 9, respectively. The patient was net negative at 10.9 L during his inpatient stay. Additionally, antinuclear, antiglomerular basement membrane, myeloperoxidase, and serine protease‐3 antibodies were negative. He was discharged home 10 days after presentation with outpatient follow‐up. Eventually, ELISA testing for hantavirus IgM and IgG returned positive from a reference laboratory about 10 days after presentation, confirming the diagnosis of HCPS. Chest CT two days after bilateral chest tube insertion and diuresis showed improvement with scattered ground‐glass opacities and decreased small bilateral pleural effusions. Trends in laboratory results during the patient’s hospital stay reflect the transition from cardiopulmonary phase to convalescence. The patient was extubated and vasopressors were stopped on day 5. Right and left chest tubes were removed on day 8 and 9, respectively. 3. Discussion Since the initial recognition of HCPS during the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, approximately 30 cases have been reported annually in the United States. HCPS most commonly affects previously healthy young adults with occupational or environmental rodent exposure. Over 20 strains of hantaviruses can cause HCPS, but the primary culprits are Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus in North and South America, respectively. Rodents excrete hantaviruses in saliva, urine, and feces, and humans are infected when inhaling the secreted viruses or rarely by rodent bites. This case illustrates a classical but diagnostically challenging presentation of HCPS in a young ranch worker with substantial exposure to rodent‐contaminated environments. 3.1. Gastrointestinal‐Predominant Prodrome as a Diagnostic Pitfall The incubation period of hantavirus ranges from 1 to 3 weeks. The prodromal phase of HCPS frequently resembles a nonspecific viral or gastrointestinal illness and may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea before overt respiratory symptoms develop. Gastrointestinal‐predominant presentations may delay diagnosis because clinicians often initially prioritize gastroenteritis, abdominal sepsis, arboviral disease, or other infectious syndromes. In this case, several bedside “red flags” increased suspicion for HCPS despite the nonspecific prodrome: severe thrombocytopenia, marked hemoconcentration, granulocytic left shift, rapid respiratory deterioration, and rodent exposure in an endemic region. Clinicians at the University of New Mexico developed five criteria to guide clinical decisions and make a presumptive diagnosis during this phase: thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, granulocytic left shift, absence of toxic changes, and more than 10% immunoblasts. Blood smears meeting four of five criteria had high sensitivity (96%), specificity (99%), and positive predictive value (83%) for infection. Notably, our patient met the criteria, and confirmatory testing for hantavirus was dispatched at this stage. 3.2. Differential Diagnosis and Early Clinical Decision‐Making This case highlights two critical clinical decision‐making windows. During the initial prodromal phase, differential considerations included viral gastroenteritis, leptospirosis, dengue/arboviral infections, bacterial sepsis, rickettsioses, influenza‐like illness, Epstein–Barr virus, human bocavirus, hematologic malignancies, and abdominal sources of infection. As the patient progressed to respiratory failure and shock, the differential expanded to include severe sepsis‐associated ARDS, vasculitis with diffuse alveolar injury or pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Goodpasture syndrome), Aspergillus, Pneumocystis, Legionella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Q fever, and HCPS. Several features substantially increased the likelihood of HCPS: rapid onset pulmonary edema with preserved cardiac function, thrombocytopenia, marked hemoconcentration, diffuse capillary leak, and epidemiologic exposure to rodent‐contaminated ranch environments. The broad diagnostic evaluation was appropriate because early HCPS frequently mimics other severe infectious and inflammatory syndromes. 3.3. Pathophysiology of Capillary Leak and Pulmonary Edema Pathogenesis of hantavirus infection is characterized by increased vascular permeability, as the virus principally targets endothelial cells of pulmonary and renal capillaries. It is hypothesized that alpha and beta‐3 integrins act as hantavirus receptors on endothelial cells, and their inactivation contributes to the deregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor, leading to altered expression and internalization of vascular endothelial cadherins, damaging the endothelial barrier. In HCPS, this accounts for the capillary leak syndrome by pulmonary edema, pleural effusions, hemoconcentration, hypotension, ascites, mesenteric edema, and anasarca, all of which were present in this patient. Thrombocytopenia is a common and early marker of disease severity and is thought to result from increased endothelial activation and consumption. Although echocardiography demonstrated preserved ventricular systolic function, BNP elevation raised consideration of transient myocardial involvement, which has been described in HCPS. Therefore, pulmonary edema in HCPS may reflect a mixed process involving both severe endothelial leak and variable myocardial depression. In this case, preserved ventricular function and the overall hemodynamic pattern favored predominantly noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. 3.4. Risk Stratification and Escalation of Care This patient presented with several features associated with severe HCPS, including profound thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, vasopressor‐dependent shock, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, diffuse pulmonary edema, and elevated lactate levels. These high‐risk features justified early transfer to an ECMO center and close hemodynamic monitoring. Despite his severe presentation, the patient experienced favorable recovery without ECMO support. Potential explanations include early recognition of capillary leak physiology, prompt intensive care support, lung‐protective ventilation, vasopressor therapy, conservative fluid management, patient age, gender, and the absence of significant medical comorbidities. Recent systematic review data emphasize the importance of early referral to an ECMO center for advanced supportive therapies in severe HCPS. 3.5. Current and Emerging Therapies Management of HCPS remains largely supportive. Mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic support, conservative fluid management, and early recognition of capillary leak physiology are central to care. Venoarterial ECMO may be used in cases with cardiac index < 2.5 L/minute/m2 despite pressor and inotropic support. Small placebo‐controlled studies using ribavirin or high‐dose methylprednisolone did not show clear benefits. A nonrandomized pre‐ and postintervention study (ISRCTN72088243) to assess the efficacy of tocilizumab in reducing mortality in HCPS is underway in Argentina. A recent case‐series based on this trial seemed to show some promise for IL‐6 inhibition in four of the five HCPS patients who survived to ICU discharge after treatment with tocilizumab. However, given the high mortality and a lack of established treatment options, prevention of hantavirus infection by implementing measures to limit contact with rodents is of utmost importance. 3.6. Epidemiology and Long‐Term Outcomes Arizona and the broader Four Corners region remain endemic areas for Sin Nombre virus transmission because of persistent deer mouse reservoirs and environmental exposure risks in rural settings. Occupational exposure involving barns, feed storage areas, sweeping of rodent‐contaminated spaces, and aerosolization of rodent excreta remain important risk factors for infection. Long‐term outcomes among HCPS survivors remain incompletely characterized. Although many patients recover functional independence, persistent fatigue, exertional intolerance, and psychological distress have been reported after severe disease. In this case, the patient demonstrated favorable short‐term recovery and was able to return to routine activities within weeks of discharge, although mild exertional fatigue persisted at follow‐up. 4. Conclusion The strength of this case report lies in serologic confirmation of Hantavirus using ELISA and elaborate clinical details on its presentation, complications, and management. Although it is limited to a single patient, it underscores the diagnostic complexity and clinical severity of HCPS. Notably, gastrointestinal‐predominant prodromal symptoms may obscure early recognition and delay diagnosis. Although rare, HCPS should remain high on the differential for patients presenting with hemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, rapid‐onset respiratory failure, and shock, especially in endemic regions with known rodent exposure. Early risk stratification, aggressive supportive management, and timely referral to centers capable of advanced cardiopulmonary support are essential to optimize outcomes. analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is a rare but frequently fatal viral disease endemic to the Americas, transmitted primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta.
analysis.methods: A single 20‑year‑old man from southwestern Arizona was evaluated; clinical data were collected during hospitalization and diagnosis was confirmed with a serum ELISA positive for hantavirus IgM and IgG.
analysis.results: The patient presented with gastrointestinal symptoms, then rapidly developed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/µL), septic shock, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, required intubation, vasopressor support, and chest CT showed pulmonary edema with large bilateral pleural effusions; he improved with supportive care, was extubated, discharged home, and ELISA confirmed hantavirus infection.
analysis.contribution: The case highlights diagnostic complexity when gastrointestinal prodromes dominate, emphasizes that hemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and rapid respiratory failure should raise suspicion for HCPS, and reinforces supportive care as the mainstay while noting potential benefit of ECMO referral.
analysis.limitations: As a single‑patient case report, the findings are not generalizable and lack comparative data; no formal IRB review was required.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS is a rare but often fatal disease transmitted via rodent aerosols. Methods: One 20‑year‑old man in southwestern Arizona was assessed and diagnosed by hantavirus IgM/IgG ELISA. Results: He progressed from GI symptoms to hemoconcentration (Hct 58%), thrombocytopenia (17,000 cells/µL), shock, pulmonary edema, required ventilation and vasopressors, showed CT evidence of large pleural effusions, improved with supportive care, and tested positive for hantavirus. Contribution: The report underscores diagnostic challenges with GI‑predominant prodrome, the importance of early suspicion based on lab abnormalities, and supportive care with possible ECMO referral. Limitations: Single‑case design limits broader applicability.

papers.title_zh: 关于美国西南部汉坦病毒毛细血管漏综合征的病例报告。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)是一种罕见但常致命的病毒性疾病,流行于美洲,主要通过吸入鼠类排泄物的气溶胶传播。
analysis_zh.methods: 对一名来自亚利桑那州西南部的20岁男性进行评估;在住院期间收集临床资料,诊断通过血清ELISA检测到汉坦病毒 IgM和IgG阳性得到确认。
analysis_zh.results: 患者出现胃肠道症状,随后迅速出现血液浓缩(血红蛋白压积58%),血小板减少(17,000/μL),脓毒性休克,非心源性肺水肿,需要气管插管和血管加压药支持,胸部CT显示肺水肿伴大面积双侧胸腔积液;经支持治疗后病情好转,拔管出院,ELISA确认汉坦病毒感染。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该病例凸显了胃肠先兆占主导时的诊断复杂性,强调血液浓缩、血小板减少和快速呼吸衰竭应提高对HCPS的警觉,并重申支持治疗是核心,同时指出转诊至体外膜氧合(ECMO)可能有益。
analysis_zh.limitations: 作为单例病例报告,研究结果不可推广且缺乏对照数据;无需正式的伦理审查(IRB)。

papers.title: Hantavirus on a Cruise Ship: What COVID-19 Taught Us.
papers.abstract: Delayed recognition of the mechanics of aerosol transmission-the primary mode of spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-at the beginning of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic led to inadequate early recommendations regarding nonpharmaceutical interventions and poor initial messaging about how to reduce infection risk. We highlight key epidemiological details of Andes virus (ANDV) transmission on the MV Hondius cruise ship and during prior reported outbreaks with confirmed person-to-person spread in Argentina, which, together, suggest aerosol spread may be a key mechanism of transmission of ANDV between source cases and susceptible contacts in permissible environmental settings.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

papers.title: Hantavirus: An Emerging Global Zoonotic Threat—From Molecular Basis to Clinical Management and Public Health Perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonotic viral disease caused by hantaviruses of the family Hantaviridae, primarily transmitted to humans through exposure to infected rodent urine, feces, saliva, or contaminated aerosols. The disease presents mainly in two clinical forms: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), prevalent in Asia and Europe, and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS)/Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas. The historical recognition of hantavirus began during the Korean War (1950–1953), when thousands of soldiers developed Korean hemorrhagic fever. In 1978, Ho-Wang Lee isolated the Hantaan virus from Apodemus agrarius, marking a major scientific breakthrough. Subsequent decades witnessed the identification of multiple hantavirus species, including Seoul, Puumala, Dobrava-Belgrade, Sin Nombre, and Andes viruses, each associated with distinct rodent reservoirs and clinical manifestations. A major epidemiological milestone occurred in 1993 with the outbreak of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome in the Four Corners region of the United States, leading to the discovery of Sin Nombre virus. Increasing urbanization, climate change, deforestation, and closer human–rodent interactions have contributed to the global emergence of hantavirus infections in the 21st century. Advances in molecular diagnostics, including reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and serological testing, have enhanced disease surveillance and early diagnosis. This review highlights the historical evolution, epidemiology, transmission, and growing public health significance of hantavirus infection worldwide. Keywords: Hantavirus infection; Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS); Hantavirus Pulmonary

A major epidemiological milestone occurred in 1993 with the outbreak of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome in the Four Corners region of the United States, leading to the discovery of Sin Nombre virus. Increasing urbanization, climate change, deforestation, and closer human–rodent interactions have contributed to the global emergence of hantavirus infections in the 21st century. Introduction Hantavirus infection is a zoonotic disease associated primarily with small mammals and remains an important cause of severe acute febrile illness in regions where pathogenic orthohantaviruses circulate. Human infection is usually acquired through contact with an infected reservoir host or through inhalation of virus-containing material generated from rodent urine, feces, saliva, or nesting material. The epidemiology is highly focal because individual viral lineages are often maintained within particular reservoir species, and human risk therefore changes with habitat, rodent density, occupational exposure, seasonality, land use, and human behavior. The two major clinical syndromes are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary or cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS), which differ in the dominant organs involved but share important pathophysiological features centered on vascular permeability and dysregulated host responses [1]. The modern understanding of hantavirus disease has evolved from outbreak recognition to molecular epidemiology and systems-level surveillance. The discovery of Hantaan virus in the late twentieth century established the rodent reservoir connection, while the 1993 outbreak in the southwestern United States and identification of Sin Nombre virus established HPS as a distinct severe clinical entity in the Americas. Subsequent studies demonstrated extensive viral and ecological diversity, including the ability of Andes virus to undergo limited person-to- person transmission under conditions of close and prolonged exposure. Current taxonomy places the mammalian human-pathogenic viruses within the family Hantaviridae, subfamily Mammantavirinae, and genus Orthohantavirus, reflecting a broader understanding of hantavirid diversity than the older classification systems used in many clinical reviews [2]. Despite improved laboratory diagnostics and supportive critical care, hantavirus infection remains difficult to manage because the clinical deterioration of severe disease can be rapid and no globally licensed curative antiviral therapy is available. This review therefore examines the disease as an integrated ecological, virological, clinical, and public-health problem. Particular emphasis is placed on mechanisms that connect viral entry and replication with endothelial dysfunction, organ-specific syndromes, diagnostic decision-making, treatment limitations, vaccine development, and the growing importance of genomic and One Health surveillance [3]. 2. Historical Background and Discovery 2.1 Early Recognition and the Korean Hemorrhagic Fever Era The clinical syndrome now recognized as HFRS drew major international attention during the Korean War, when thousands of United Nations soldiers developed an acute febrile illness accompanied by renal dysfunction, hemorrhagic manifestations, hypotension, and shock [4]. The disease was initially described as Korean hemorrhagic fever, and the geographic association with the Hantaan River became an important clue to its natural history. Although the outbreak produced a strong epidemiological signal, the etiological agent remained elusive for decades because the disease was associated with an environmentally acquired infection that did not fit the conventional models of human-to-human viral transmission [5]. A decisive breakthrough came in 1978 when Ho-Wang Lee and colleagues isolated the etiological virus from the striped field mouse, Apodemus agrarius, in the region of the Hantaan River. This finding established a durable link between pathogenic hantaviruses and persistent infection in rodent hosts and created the basis for ecological surveillance. The discovery also clarified why human disease was geographically patterned and why rodent abundance, habitat disturbance, and occupational exposure could alter risk without requiring sustained transmission between people [6]. 2.2 Expansion of Hantavirus Discovery and Classification Following the identification of Hantaan virus, related viruses were recognized in multiple regions and linked to distinct reservoir hosts. Seoul virus was associated with commensal rats and demonstrated a distribution compatible with urban exposure, whereas Puumala virus became closely associated with nephropathia epidemica, a comparatively milder form of HFRS in northern and central Europe. Dobrava-associated disease was recognized as another severe HFRS phenotype in parts of southeastern Europe. The expanding catalogue showed that hantavirus ecology is structured by host-virus relationships rather than by geography alone [7]. The current taxonomic framework further reflects this diversity. ICTV classifies Hantaviridae within the class Bunyaviricetes and order Elliovirales; mammalian hantaviruses are distributed across several genera, while human disease is associated with Orthohantavirus. The genome architecture is conserved across the family, but viral sequence Review Article 492 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) variation, glycoprotein properties, reservoir adaptation, and host-response differences contribute to species-specific ecological and clinical phenotypes. This modern classification is important because older descriptions based only on a few rodent-borne viruses can underestimate the breadth of hantavirid diversity [8]. 2.3 Emergence of Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome In 1993, an outbreak in the Four Corners region of the United States was characterized by rapidly progressive respiratory failure in previously healthy individuals. Investigation identified a previously unrecognized hantavirus that was subsequently named Sin Nombre virus and traced to the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus. The event established HPS as a severe pulmonary syndrome distinct from the renal- predominant disease recognized in Eurasia. It also demonstrated the value of integrating clinical observation, epidemiology, molecular virology, and wildlife investigation during an unexplained outbreak [9]. The discovery of Andes virus and subsequent South American outbreaks provided additional insight into hantavirus transmission. Unlike most pathogenic hantaviruses, Andes virus has repeatedly been associated with limited human-to-human transmission among close contacts. This phenotype does not represent sustained community transmission; rather, it highlights a specific transmission capability that becomes epidemiologically relevant when close contact occurs during the period of high clinical infectivity [10]. 2.4 Hantavirus in the Twenty-First Century Twenty-first-century hantavirus surveillance increasingly recognizes that emergence is shaped by interactions among ecological change, host population dynamics, climate variability, land-use change, mobility, and diagnostic capacity. Urbanization may increase contact with commensal rodents, while deforestation and agricultural expansion can alter wildlife interfaces. Climate-related changes can influence rodent population abundance and movement in some ecosystems, but the relationship is nonlinear and depends on local precipitation, food availability, predator dynamics, and habitat structure. Consequently, environmental change should be viewed as a set of modifiers of transmission opportunity rather than as a single causal driver [11]. A particularly instructive recent event occurred in 2026 in association with the MV Hondius expedition cruise. The outbreak was identified after severe respiratory illness among passengers and crew and was attributed to Andes virus. By 2 July 2026, WHO reported 13 linked cases, including 12 laboratory- confirmed cases and one probable case, with three deaths. All identified cases were among people who had travelled on the vessel. The investigation supported a point-source introduction followed by limited secondary person-to-person transmission, and WHO reported that the outbreak was contained with no further related transmission expected. The event illustrates how a pathogen that ordinarily depends on zoonotic exposure can create a short-lived international public-health challenge when infected individuals enter a confined travel setting [12]. 3. Virology and Molecular Characteristics 3.1 Taxonomy and Virion Architecture Hantaviridae is a diverse family of enveloped negative- sense RNA viruses. The current ICTV framework places the family in the realm Riboviria, kingdom Orthornavirae, phylum Negarnaviricota, class Bunyaviricetes, and order Elliovirales. Mammalian hantavirids occur in several genera, but the human pathogenic viruses currently recognized belong to Orthohantavirus. The virion is generally pleomorphic and approximately 80–160 nm in diameter, with an envelope containing the Gn and Gc glycoproteins arranged as surface spikes. These glycoproteins mediate attachment, entry, and important antigenic interactions with the host immune system [13]. The association of specific orthohantaviruses with particular rodent or other small-mammal reservoirs is a defining ecological feature. Reservoir infection is generally persistent and clinically inapparent, suggesting long-term host adaptation. In humans, however, the outcome can range from mild or nonspecific illness to rapidly progressive HFRS or HCPS. The disconnect between apparently benign reservoir infection and severe human disease emphasizes that pathogenicity depends on both viral properties and the context of spillover into an immunologically different host [14]. 3.2 Genome Organization and Viral Proteins Orthohantaviruses possess a tripartite, negative-sense RNA genome comprising small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, which binds genomic RNA and participates in ribonucleoprotein organization and replication. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor that is processed into Gn and Gc, the principal envelope proteins. The L segment encodes the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which carries out transcription and replication of the segmented genome. Viral mRNAs are capped but not polyadenylated, and cap-snatching from host cellular mRNAs contributes to efficient transcription [15]. Review Article 493 Current Pharmaceutical Research (CPR) The tripartite architecture is biologically consequential because replication depends on coordinated packaging and synthesis of three distinct RNA segments. Segment reassortment and sequence variation can alter viral phenotype and complicate molecularsurveillance. At the same time, conserved structural and enzymatic functions provide targets for diagnostic assay design, antibody development, antiviral screening, and vaccine engineering. Understanding the relationships among N, Gn/Gc, and polymerase functions therefore remains central to translating virological knowledge into clinical and public-health applications [16]. 3.3 Viral Entry, Replication, and Cellular Tropism Hantavirus attachment and entry involve interactions between viral glycoproteins and host-cell receptors, with beta-3 integrins representing an important component of the receptor biology described for pathogenic hantaviruses. Endothelial cells are a major cellular target, yet infection of these cells does not typically produce the extensive direct cytolysis that characterizes some other viral diseases. Instead, hantavirus replication occurs in the setting of altered endothelial signaling, cytoskeletal regulation, junctional integrity, platelet interactions, and inflammatory mediator release. This helps explain why dramatic vascular leakage can coexist with relatively limited structural destruction of the endothelial monolayer [17]. After entry, the negative-sense RNA genome must be transcribed by the viral polymerase before viral proteins can be produced. Newly synthesized ribonucleoprotein complexes and glycoproteins are assembled through coordinated intracellular trafficking, followed by budding and release of progeny virions. The precise contribution of individual host pathways to severe disease continues to be investigated, but current models emphasize that pathogenicity emerges from the combination of viral replication, host-cell signaling, complement and coagulation pathways, platelet-endothelial interactions, and innate and adaptive immune responses [18]. 4. Reservoirs and Transmission 4.1 Reservoir Ecology Rodents constitute the principal reservoir hosts for the orthohantaviruses that cause human disease, with many viral lineages showing a close association with particular host species. Examples include Apodemus species for Hantaan virus, Rattus species for Seoul virus, bank voles for Puumala virus, and Peromyscus maniculatus for Sin Nombre virus. Andes virus is associated with sigmodontine rodents in South America. Reservoir specificity helps shape geographic distribution and also means that changes in host abundance or habitat can alter human exposure even when the virus itself has not changed [19]. Reservoir surveillance is therefore more informative when it integrates virological detection with ecological measurements such as rodent density, reproductive cycles, vegetation, food availability, habitat fragmentation, and human land use. From a One Health perspective, spillover should be understood as the outcome of a connected system involving reservoir competence, environmental contamination, human behavior, and access to health services [20]. 4.2 Routes of Transmission to Humans Most human infections result from exposure to infectious rodent excreta or contaminated environmental material. Aerosolization is particularly relevant when dried urine, feces, or nesting material is disturbed during sweeping, cleaning, construction, farming, or entry into enclosed spaces. Transmission may also occur when contaminated material contacts mucous membranes or broken skin. Rodent bites and scratches are possible but are less common routes. Ingestion of contaminated food or water is biologically plausible but is less clearly established than inhalational or direct mucosal exposure [21]. The incubation period is variable and generally spans approximately one to eight weeks, depending on the virus and exposure context. Because the early clinical syndrome is nonspecific, a history of rodent exposure often provides the epidemiological clue that makes targeted laboratory testing appropriate. Exposure assessment should therefore include home and workplace conditions, cleaning activities, agricultural or forestry work, travel to endemic regions, and direct contact with rodents or rodent-contaminated materials [22]. 4.3 Human-to-Human Transmission Person-to-person transmission is not a general feature of hantavirus infection. The best-established example is Andes virus, for which limited transmission has been documented among household members, intimate contacts, and healthcare-associated close contacts. Available observations indicate that prolonged, close contact during the early clinical phase is particularly relevant. Other pathogenic hantaviruses have not demonstrated comparable sustained…
