papers.title: Evaluation of Andes virus vaccine-derived human antibody for protection in Syrian hamsters: a passive transfer study using phase 1 trial sera.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) causes severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and is uniquely capable of person-to-person transmission, with no licenced vaccines or therapeutics available. A Phase 1 trial (NCT03682107) demonstrated that an ANDV DNA vaccine targeting Gn/Gc envelope proteins elicits neutralising antibodies in humans. We evaluated whether these human antibodies protect against lethal disease in an animal model. METHODS: Day 197 sera from vaccinated human subjects were pooled, purified, and passively transferred to female Syrian hamsters one day prior to lethal ANDV challenge across two independent experiments. Controls included normal human IgG, PBS (negative controls), and SAB-400 (positive control). Neutralising antibody levels were quantified using pseudovirion neutralisation assays (PsVNA) and plaque reduction neutralisation tests (PRNT) to determine exploratory cutoff titres predicting survival. FINDINGS: Human antibodies from DNA-vaccinated subjects-unlike normal IgG-conferred significant protection against lethal ANDV challenge in both experiments. The exploratory cutoff titres predicting protection were determined to be 31-184 for PsVNA50 and 20-80 for PRNT50, depending on the analysis population and model parameters. INTERPRETATION: Vaccine-induced human antibodies are sufficient to protect against lethal ANDV infection in an established animal model. If confirmed, these results indicate that neutralising antibody titres could serve as a surrogate endpoint and correlate of protection for future hantavirus Gn/Gc-targeted vaccines. FUNDING: Defense Health Program and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

analysis_zh.methods: 来自 DNA 疫苗接种人受试者的第 197 天血清被合并、纯化,并在致死性 ANDV 挑战前一天被动转移至雌性叙利亚仓鼠,进行两项独立实验 (A4);对照组为普通人类 IgG、PBS(阴性)和 SAB‐400(阳性) (A5);通过假病毒颗粒中和实验 (PsVNA) 和斑块还原中和试验 (PRNT) 测定中和抗体水平,以探索保护性滴度阈值 (A6)。

analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,疫苗诱导的人类抗体能够保护已建立的动物模型免受致死性 ANDV 感染 (A9),并提示中和抗体滴度可作为未来 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 靶向疫苗的替代终点和保护相关性指标 (A10)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要和部分正文;未报告详细的样本量、统计分析以及更广泛的人体安全性或有效性数据。

papers.title: Dual-Target Inhibition of Puumala Virus Entry Glycoproteins Gn and Gc by Moringa oleifera -Derived Phytochemicals: An Integrated Computational Study
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), a member of the Orthohantavirus genus, causes nephropathia epidemica, an intermediate type of hemorrhagic fever with renal dysfunction, yet no approved antiviral therapy is currently available. Viral entry is initiated by the coordinated actions of the attachment glycoprotein Gn and fusion glycoprotein Gc, making simultaneous inhibition of these proteins an attractive antiviral strategy. Here, we employed a combined computational workflow to identify dual-target inhibitors of PUUV entry glycoproteins from Moringa oleifera phytochemicals. 72 phytochemicals were retrieved and docked by molecular docking to identify high-affinity binders, while he top-ranked compounds were subsequently evaluated for drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic behavior, toxicity, and predicted biological activities to assess their therapeutic suitability. analysis.background: Puumala virus (PUUV) causes nephropathia epidemica, an intermediate hemorrhagic fever with renal dysfunction, and no approved antiviral therapy exists.
analysis.methods: An integrated computational workflow retrieved 72 Moringa oleifera phytochemicals, docked them to PUUV Gn and Gc glycoproteins, screened top hits for drug‑likeness and pharmacokinetics, and examined complex stability with 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations and MM‑GBSA binding free‑energy calculations.
analysis.results: Quercetin and kaempferol displayed the lowest docking energies (−9.8/−9.7 kcal/mol for Gn and −10.4/−10.0 kcal/mol for Gc) and the most favorable MM‑GBSA free energies (−84.24 and −98.45 kcal/mol), with MD simulations confirming stable protein–ligand complexes.
analysis.contribution: The work proposes quercetin and kaempferol as promising dual‑target inhibitors that could simultaneously block PUUV attachment and membrane fusion, offering computational leads for antiviral development.
analysis.limitations: Results are derived solely from in silico analyses presented in an abstract; experimental validation and in‑vivo efficacy have not been demonstrated.

papers.title_zh: 通过Moringa oleifera来源的植物化学物质对普马拉病毒进入糖蛋白Gn和Gc的双靶点抑制:一项综合计算研究

analysis_zh.background: 普马拉病毒 (普马拉病毒) 引起肾病流行性,这是一种伴有肾功能障碍的中间型肾综合征出血热,且目前尚无获批的抗病毒疗法。
analysis_zh.methods: 通过一套集成的计算工作流,检索了 72 种辣木(Moringa oleifera)植物化学成分,将其对接至普马拉病毒 Gn 与 Gc 糖蛋白,筛选出具备药物相似性和药代动力学特性的高分子,并利用 100 ns 分子动力学模拟及 MM‐GBSA 结合自由能计算评估复合物的稳定性。
analysis_zh.results: 槲皮素和山柰酚表现出最低的对接能(Gn 为 −9.8/−9.7 kcal/mol,Gc 为 −10.4/−10.0 kcal/mol)以及最有利的 MM‐GBSA 结合自由能(分别为 −84.24 kcal/mol 和 −98.45 kcal/mol),分子动力学模拟进一步证实了蛋白‐配体复合物的稳定性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提出槲皮素和山柰酚作为有前景的双靶点抑制剂,可同时阻断普马拉病毒的附着和膜融合,为抗病毒药物研发提供计算线索。
analysis_zh.limitations: 结果仅基于摘要中呈现的体外计算分析,尚未进行实验验证或体内疗效评估。

papers.title: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving outcomes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratification. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine laboratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS.

papers.full_text: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome Xiaojiao Li 1,2,3, Lin Su 2,3, Yinli He 2,3, Linpei Zhang 2,3, Tianyan Chen 1*, Minhong Fei 4* and Yawen Wang 2,3,5* 1Infectious Diseases Department, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 2BioBank, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 3Shaanxi Engineering Research Center for Biobank and Advanced Medical Research, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 4Jiangyan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Taizhou, Jiangsu, China, 5Department of Laboratory Medicine, First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving out- comes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratifi- cation. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine labo- ratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Immunological markers provide mechanistic insight that also supports early identification of severe HFRS, as reflected by a core cytokine imbalance, impaired antigen-specific T- and B-cell responses, and aberrant activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and the complement system. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS. KEYWORDS biomarkers, early warning indicators, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, risk stratification, severe HFRS 1 Introduction Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute infectious disease caused by several Orthohantavirus species in the family Hantaviridae. Human infection usually occurs through inhalation of aerosolized virus from the excreta of infected rodents (1). The main causative viral strains differ by geographic region. Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are major causes of HFRS in Asia. HTNV infection may be associated with case fatality rates of approximately 5%–15%, whereas SEOV infection is generally milder. Puumala virus (PUUV) predominates in Europe and generally causes a milder form known as nephropathia epidemica (NE), with a case fatality rate of 0.1% to 0.4%. China accounts for >90% of the global HFRS burden, with more than 1.62 million cases and nearly 47,000 deaths from 1950 to 2014 (4). During 2014–2023, 91,388 total cases were reported, corre- sponding to an average annual incidence of 0.65/100,000 (5). Hantaviruses enter host cells primarily by binding to b3 integrins on the surface of endothelial cells (6, 7). Instead of directly lysing endothelial cells, viral infection initiates a strong innate and adaptive immune response, along with an inflammatory cascade. This results in endothelial barrier dysfunction, which can be clinically observed as increased vascular permeability, thrombocytopenia, coagulation dis- turbances, and acute kidney injury (AKI) (8, 9). Clinically, HFRS classically manifests five sequential phases: the febrile phase, hypotensive shock phase, oliguric phase, diuretic phase, and convalescent phase. Not all patients experience every phase in complete sequence; phase overlap frequently occurs, in which features of two or more phases appear simultaneously (10). HFRS can be classified into four grades: mild, moderate, severe, and critical. In clinical practice, mild and moderate cases are often grouped together as a broad “mild” category, while severe and critical cases are grouped as “severe” (7, 11–13). However, the criteria for severe disease are not fully consistent across different hantavirus infections. For HTNV infection, severe HFRS is defined by a body temperature >40 °C, neurological symptoms, shock, oliguria lasting ≥5 days or anuria lasting ≥2 days, or hemorrhage in vital organs (10, 14). For PUUV-induced nephropathia epidemica (NE), severe cases are often characterized by severe AKI or shock (15, 16). Despite these differences, the definitions all highlight the essential features of severe HFRS, including hypotension or shock, severe AKI, a significant bleeding tendency, and multiple organ dysfunction (17). Currently, no specific antiviral therapy is available, and the management of severe HFRS relies mainly on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), mechan- ical ventilation, and vasopressor support (12, 17, 18). However, because of rapid progression to severe disease and the limited therapeutic window, intervention is often delayed, resulting in high mortality rates (14). Therefore, early recognition of patients at risk of severe progression and prompt initiation of intensive care are critical for improving outcomes. In recent years, research on early warning of severe HFRS has advanced considerably across multiple levels, encompassing bedside signs, routine laboratory parameters, immunological markers, and emerging novel biomarkers. In this review, we comprehensively synthesize progress in the aforementioned areas and evaluate the predictive performance and translational potential of various bio- markers. We also discuss current challenges and future perspec- tives, with the aim of establishing an evidence base for early identification and precise management of severe HFRS. 2 Clinically accessible warning systems for early risk stratification Clinically accessible warning systems including bedside signs and routine laboratory parameters are the most important indicators for predicting severe HFRS. This section reviews the available evidence on bedside signs and standard laboratory tests for predicting severe HFRS. The goal is to provide a practical frame- work for early risk assessment. 2.1 Bedside signs of severe HFRS prediction Bedside signs offer unique discriminative value for early risk stratification in HFRS, particularly in the absence of laboratory data. The 2021 Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Treatment of HFRS identifies several key warning indicators for severe cases. These include a history of travel to endemic areas or contact with rodents and their excreta within two months prior to onset, high fever (temperature >40 °C or febrile duration exceeding one week), severe gastrointestinal symptoms such as intense nausea and vomiting, psychiatric disturbances including agitation or delirium, marked conjunctival edema, and obvious bleeding tendency (10). Regarding imaging findings, a retrospective analysis by Huang et al. of 191 patients with HFRS in southwestern China demonstrated that pleural effusion was an independent risk factor for progression to severe HFRS. Patients with pleural effusion had a 4.49-fold higher risk of severe progression compared to those without it, suggesting that this sign may reflect more extensive capillary leakage and systemic inflammation (14). The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score also has shown significant value in predicting severe HFRS. Ma and colleagues conducted a multicenter study of 551 HFRS patients in Hubei Province. They demonstrated that an admission qSOFA score of 2 or higher was an independent risk factor for 30-day mortality. The qSOFA score is defined as meeting any two of the following criteria: respiratory rate ≥22 breaths/min, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, or altered mental status. This finding suggests that the qSOFA score, without reliance on any laboratory tests, can serve as a rapid triage tool for early identification of high- risk HFRS patients and for determining the need for intensive care unit admission (19). Notably, the early warning indicators for severe HFRS vary across different age groups. Researchers at Tangdu Hospital have conducted stratified warning analyses for both older adults and children (20, 21). In the older-adult cohort (≥60 years), Li et al. reviewed 146 cases and identified several early warning signs using multivariate logistic regression. These included chest tightness or dyspnea, nausea or vomiting, decreased urine output (UO), skin and mucosal hemorrhage, and phase overlap (disease course span- ning two or more typical phases). These findings suggest that assessment of older adults with HFRS should focus more on cardiopulmonary function, gastrointestinal symptoms, renal perfu- sion, coagulation status, and disease progression patterns (20). In the pediatric cohort (<16 years), the same group analyzed 103 cases. They found that conjunctival edema, hypotensive shock, and elevated serum creatinine (Cr) were key early warning indicators. This suggests that assessment in children should focus more on fluid extravasation, circulatory status, and early renal changes. Taken together, risk assessment should combine exposure history, consensus-based warning signs, bedside scores, and age-specific findings (21). Li et al. 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1986264 Frontiers in Immunology frontiersin.org 02 2.2 Routine laboratory parameters for early warning of severe HFRS 2.2.1 Blood cell indices and inflammatory markers Blood count and routine inflammatory markers are the most accessible laboratory indicators for evaluating the systemic host response in HFRS. Markedly elevated white blood cell count (WBC) and severely reduced platelet count (PLT) have long been recog- nized as warning signs for HFRS severity (11, 22). The 2021 Expert Consensus has established WBC >30 × 109/L and PLT <20 × 109/L as definitive severity warning thresholds (10). This pattern has been consistently confirmed by multiple retrospective cohort studies from various regions. Yang et al. analyzed 109 HFRS cases in central China and found that the median WBC in the severe group (25.2 × 109/L) was significantly higher than in the mild group (12.6 × 109/L), while the median PLT (22 × 109/L) was significantly lower than in the mild group (54 × 109/L) (12). Chen et al. further examined the association between these two indicators and adverse outcomes in a cohort of 395 HFRS patients in northwestern China. The results showed that the median WBC in the non-survivor group (23.19 × 109/L) was significantly higher than in the survivor group (13.29 × 109/L), while the median PLT (22 × 109/L) was significantly lower than in the survivor group (41 × 109/L) (23). Platelet distribution width (PDW) may provide infor- mation on platelet activation and function beyond that conveyed by PLT alone. Fan et al. studied 260 HFRS patients and found that PDW on the first day of admission increased significantly with disease severity. Of note, in critically ill patients, the association between PDW and prognosis was reversed, with non-survivors exhibiting lower PDW than survivors. This reversal may reflect exhausted marrow hematopoietic compensation, where declining PDW portends worse outcomes (24). The neutrophil-to-red blood cell ratio (NRR) and neutrophil- to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), as simple readouts of systemic inflam- mation, have demonstrated predictive value across multiple viral species. Xiao et al. analyzed 342 HTNV-HFRS cases in Xi’an and found that NRR was significantly elevated in the severe/critical group, with optimal discriminative performance for severity grad- ing, whereas NLR was significantly elevated in the non-survivor group, with optimal performance for 28-day all-cause mortality prediction. Both markers are accessible at the bedside, with NRR more suitable for early severity stratification and NLR better aligned with mortality risk assessment (25). In PUUV infection, Nusshag et al. analyzed 32 PUUV-infected patients in Germany and showed that peak NLR was significantly elevated in severe patients with hospitalization exceeding five days, suggesting that systemic neu- trophil-lymphocyte imbalance is an important accompanying fea- ture of PUUV severity (26). Procalcitonin (PCT), as an indicator reflecting the severity of infection and inflammation, has shown predictive value across multiple independent studies. Duan et al. found that serum PCT level at emergency department admission was an independent risk factor for severe progression in HFRS patients, with the median PCT in the severe group significantly higher than in the mild group (8.12 vs. 1.39 ng/mL); an admission PCT exceeding 2.97 ng/mL demonstrated good predictive value for severity, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.862, and a sensitivity of 88.0% (27). Chen et al. found in 272 HFRS patients that admission PCT levels increased significantly with disease severity, with an AUC of 0.792 for predicting 28-day survival/ death at an optimal cutoff of 2.28 ng/mL, outperforming WBC (AUC 0.769) (28). Che et al. further confirmed in a retrospective study of 373 HFRS patients that the median admission PCT in the severe group was significantly higher than in the mild group (3.8 vs. 1.3 ng/mL), with an AUC of 0.824 for predicting severity; PCT was also significantly higher in non-survivors than in survivors (3.6 vs. 1.7 ng/mL), with an AUC of 0.737 for predicting hospital mortality (7). Huang et al. confirmed in a retrospective cohort of 191 HFRS patients in southwestern China that PCT was an independent risk factor for severe progression, with each 1 ng/mL increase in PCT associated with approximately 33% higher odds of developing severe disease (14). Yu et al. also confirmed in a cohort of 384 HFRS patients that PCT was significantly higher in the severe/ critical group than in the mild/moderate group, with multivariate logistic regression confirming elevated PCT as an independent predictor of severe progression (29). These results indicate that PCT is a useful marker for assessing both disease severity and short- term mortality in HFRS, and may help identify high-risk pa- tients early. Unlike PCT, C-reactive protein (CRP) showed limited inde- pendent value for HFRS severity prediction. Che et al. studied 373 HFRS patients and found that admission CRP was significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group (median 42.1 vs. 29.5 mg/L). However, its AUC for severity prediction was only 0.614, far below that of PCT (0.824) (7). Yang et al. also found that although the median CRP was significantly higher in the severe group than in the mild group (51.0 vs. 30.9 mg/L), CRP was deemed to lack independent incremental value during least absolute shrink- age and selection operator (LASSO) regression variable selection and was therefore not included in the final prediction model (12). Chen et al. further confirmed in 272 HFRS patients that admission CRP was elevated across all severity grades (mean approximately 30.1 to 33.96 mg/L for each group), with no statistically significant difference among the four groups, indicating that CRP does not exhibit a gradient change with disease severity. However, CRP retains potential utility in assessing secondary bacterial infection: the median CRP in the infected group was significantly higher than in the non-infected group (43.2 vs. 26.4 mg/L, p < 0.001), with an AUC of 0.588 for predicting secondary bacterial infection (p = 0.005). Although this represents moderate-to-weak performance, it is statistically significant, whereas PCT showed no discriminative capacity in this setting (28). Therefore, CRP is more suitable as an auxiliary marker for bacterial infection rather than an independent predictor of HFRS severity. The predictive role of serum albumin (ALB) and hemoglobin (Hb) remains controversial. The 2021 Expert Consensus lists serum ALB below 15 g/L as a severity warning indicator (10). full_text_sections.full_text: Early warning indicators for severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome Xiaojiao Li 1,2,3, Lin Su 2,3, Yinli He 2,3, Linpei Zhang 2,3, Tianyan Chen 1*, Minhong Fei 4* and Yawen Wang 2,3,5* 1Infectious Diseases Department, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 2BioBank, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 3Shaanxi Engineering Research Center for Biobank and Advanced Medical Research, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China, 4Jiangyan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Taizhou, Jiangsu, China, 5Department of Laboratory Medicine, First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, Shaanxi, China Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a significant public health concern, and early identification of severe cases is critical for improving out- comes. This review synthesizes recent advances in early warning indicators for severe HFRS. Clinically accessible indicators form the basis of early risk stratifi- cation. Key bedside signs such as high fever, severe gastrointestinal symptoms, altered mental status, and overt bleeding tendency, together with routine labo- ratory parameters including thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and elevated procalcitonin, have consistently shown robust predictive value for disease severity and mortality. Emerging biomarkers of endothelial barrier disruption, early renal tubular injury, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation may further enhance predictive capacity. Despite these advances, challenges remain regarding external validation and clinical translation. Future research should focus on establishing standardized, multicenter-validated early warning systems to enable precise management of severe HFRS. papers.title: Prediction of Quercetin as a Potential Modulator of HTNV-Related Host Responses: An Integrated Computational Study with Baseline Pharmacological Characterization
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen that is mainly distributed in East Asia. It is a typical example of a One Health challenge, because it persists in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in the animals but causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) when it infects humans. This study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to systematically identify early-stage HTNV-related host interaction factors, screen potential natural compounds, and predict their underlying therapeutic mechanisms. Integrative bioinformatics analysis identified CXCL10, STAT1, and IL10 as the principal upregulated core genes associated with early-stage HTNV infection. Based on these targets, six candidate natural compounds were retrieved from the HERB database. Notably, quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate, exhibiting a favorable pharmacological profile characterized by high predicted gastrointestinal absorption and an acceptable predicted toxicity profile based on in silico ADMET assessment. Functional enrichment of HTNV-related host interaction targets suggested that HTNV infection may affect multiple host pathways, including HIF-1 signaling. Network pharmacology studies suggest that quercetin may inhibit the damage caused by HTNV infection in the host by regulating the host interaction genes and related pathways associated with HTNV. Combined transcriptomic and database analyses further suggested that quercetin may modulate apoptosis through targets including AKT1, BCL2, and STAT3. In baseline pharmacological assays in uninfected HEK293T cells, quercetin showed low cytotoxicity between 3.90625 and 7.8125 μM, increased cell viability, and reduced transcription of BCL2, MAPK3, and TNF. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding poses of quercetin within HTNV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with Lys884 and Arg892 as predicted contact residues. In conclusion, these findings identify quercetin as a hypothesis-generating computational candidate for modulating HTNV-related host responses, pending experimental validation. This research framework can provide mechanistic hypotheses regarding host–pathogen interactions and potential intervention targets, thereby supporting the prevention and control of HTNV within the “One Health” framework.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen mainly distributed in East Asia, persisting in rodent reservoirs without causing disease in animals but causing severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans.
analysis.methods: The study employed an integrated bioinformatics approach to identify early‑stage HTNV‑related host interaction factors, screen natural compounds, and predict therapeutic mechanisms.
analysis.results: Core up‑regulated genes CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were identified; quercetin emerged as the most promising candidate with favorable ADMET predictions, low cytotoxicity (3.9‑7.8 µM) and increased cell viability in HEK293T cells; docking suggested favorable binding to HTNV RdRp (Lys884, Arg892).
analysis.contribution: The computational framework generates mechanistic hypotheses on host–pathogen interactions and highlights quercetin as a potential modulator, supporting One Health‑based prevention and control strategies for HTNV.
analysis.limitations: Findings are hypothesis‑generating and based solely on abstract‑level data; experimental validation of quercetin’s antiviral effects is pending.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is a rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogen in East Asia that causes severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in humans. Methods: An integrated bioinformatics workflow identified early‑stage host interaction factors, screened natural compounds, and predicted mechanisms. Results: CXCL10, STAT1 and IL10 were up‑regulated; quercetin showed favorable ADMET, low cytotoxicity (3.9‑7.8 µM) and predicted binding to HTNV RdRp. Contribution: The study provides mechanistic hypotheses and a candidate (quercetin) for HTNV modulation within a One Health context. Limitations: Conclusions are based on abstract‑only data and await experimental validation.

papers.title_zh: 预测槲皮素作为HTNV相关宿主反应潜在调节剂:基于基线药理特征的综合计算研究

analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒(HTNV)是一种主要分布于东亚的啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,持续存在于啮齿动物宿主中不致动物发病,但在人体可导致严重的肾综合征出血热。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用综合生物信息学方法,识别早期HTNV相关宿主相互作用因子,筛选天然化合物,并预测治疗机制。
analysis_zh.results: 鉴定出核心上调基因CXCL10、STAT1和IL10;槲皮素被确定为最有前景的候选物,具备良好的ADMET预测、低细胞毒性(3.9‐7.8 μM)并提升HEK293T细胞活力;分子对接显示其可与HTNV RdRp的Lys884、Arg892位点形成有利结合。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该计算框架生成宿主–病原相互作用的机制假设,并突出槲皮素作为潜在调节剂,为基于One Health的HTNV防控策略提供支持。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究结果仅为假设生成,且仅基于摘要层面的数据;槲皮素抗病毒作用的实验验证尚待开展。

papers.title: Integrated immunoinformatics and molecular dynamics approaches reveal a promising multi-epitope vaccine against hantavirus.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonotic pathogen causing Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), with substantial global morbidity and mortality. No universally approved human vaccine exists, making a safe, effective vaccine a public health priority. An immunoinformatics strategy was used to design a multi-epitope vaccine construct (MEVC) targeting the glycoprotein precursor (GP_HANTL) of Hantaan orthohantavirus. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and B-cell epitopes were predicted and screened for antigenicity, immunogenicity, MHC-binding affinity, and population coverage. Selected epitopes were joined with EAAAK, AAY, GPGPG, and KK linkers and fused to a β-defensin adjuvant. The construct was evaluated by physicochemical characterization, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, immune simulation, codon optimization, and in silico cloning. The final construct comprised 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B-cell epitopes, with 99.24% global population coverage. Structural validation showed 95% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 82. Molecular docking produced a favorable ClusPro score (- 1273.6) for the selected MEVC-TLR4 complex. Immune simulations predicted robust humoral and cellular responses, including elevated antibodies, memory B cells, and CTL/HTL activation. Codon optimization yielded a CAI of 0.94, supporting efficient Escherichia coli expression. A 100-ns MD simulation showed substantial conformational adaptation of the MEVC while TLR4 remained comparatively stable; accompanying Rg and SASA trends indicated that the MEVC adopted a more compact state during the trajectory. The proposed MEVC demonstrated favorable predicted immunogenicity, favorable structural characteristics, broad population coverage, and favorable expression characteristics. These findings support experimental validation and development of a preventive strategy against Hantavirus infection. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00782-6.

papers.title: ArHa: A globally standardised, relational database of arenavirus and hantavirus sampling in wild small mammal populations
papers.abstract: Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Efforts to map their ecological drivers and predict spillover risk are hindered by the fragmentation of historical surveillance data across the primary literature, compounded by shifting host nomenclature and variable geographic precision. We present ArHa, a database of 123,101 host occurrence and pathogen diagnostic records derived from a systematic review of published wild small mammal sampling. The dataset standardises host and pathogen taxonomies, resolves records of the same animals published in more than one paper, and classifies the spatial resolution and reliability of each coordinate to support bias-aware spatial epidemiology. To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository.

To accurately preserve complex study designs, such as multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host, ArHa is structured as a four-tier relational database. This architecture handles many-to-one relationships and supports linkage without data duplication. The dataset is distributed as compressed Apache Parquet files for programmatic analysis and as a Darwin Core Archive, so that it can be read by standard biodiversity data tools. An accompanying interactive web application, the ArHa Database Explorer, allows users to filter, visualise, and export subsets of the database without requiring programming expertise. All data, extraction scripts, and the interactive web application are openly accessible via a permanent Zenodo repository. 1.1 Keywords Hantaviridae; Arenaviridae; rodent-borne zoonoses; wildlife disease surveillance; systematic review; relational database; spatial epidemiology; Darwin Core 2. Background & Summary Arenaviruses and hantaviruses represent substantial global zoonotic threats, primarily circulating within small mammal reservoirs of the orders Rodentia and Eulipotyphla (Jonsson et al. 2010; Childs and Peters 1993). The frequency and geographic extent of zoonotic spillover are driven by complex interactions between climate, land-use change, and host community ecology (Keesing et al. 2010; Yanagihara et al. 2014; McMahon et al. 2018). Predictive spillover modelling and spatial epidemiology depend on robust, broad- scale ecological data to parameterise these environmental drivers (Kreuder Johnson et al. 2015; Olival et al. 2017; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). However, the historical surveillance data required for such analyses remain highly fragmented across decades of isolated primary literature. This fragmentation restricts the ability to construct the global datasets required for macro-ecological modelling. Compounding this fragmentation is the challenge of harmonising historical ecological data through shifting taxonomic nomenclature and inconsistent spatial reporting. Reservoir host taxonomy has undergone substantial revision over the past half-century (Kryštufek et al. 2020). Without standardisation, these taxonomic shifts can artificially separate historical ecological baselines from contemporary genomic surveillance. Further, trapping data frequently lacks high-resolution geographic coordinates, often reporting sampling locations at the provincial or district level. Treating these aggregate, district-level reports as point-level occurrence data in spatial models risks introducing analytical bias by misaligning host occurrences with high-resolution environmental covariates (Lachish and Murray 2018; Gibb, Albery, Becker, et al. 2021). The ArHa database bridges raw historical field trapping data and modern analytical pipelines. By systematically extracting, standardising, and centralising published small mammal sampling data, ArHa addresses the barriers posed by shifting host nomenclature and inconsistent spatial and temporal reporting. Each record is annotated with a categorical geographic coordinate resolution (from trapping site, village, town, city or study area, through the third, second and first administrative levels, to country) and a categorical temporal resolution (from a full date, through day, month and year ranges, to dates inferred from the publication), alongside the taxonomic resolution of the sampled animal, allowing users to filter or weight records according to the precision required. ArHa uses a relational database structure to capture the complexity of historical study designs: where single specimens yield multiple diagnostic assay results or genetic sequences, this structure preserves those relationships without the record duplication inherent to flat-file formats, providing a robust, FAIR-compliant foundation for future research. 3. Methods 3.1 Literature Search and Data Extraction Searches of NCBI PubMed and Clarivate Web of Science on 16 October 2023 returned 4,020 records; with 11 records identified by other means, 2,755 unique records remained after de-duplication (Simons et al. 2025). Briefly, the extraction process captured study design, raw trapping effort (e.g., total trap nights), diagnostic assay methodologies, and NCBI GenBank accession numbers linking host and pathogen sequences. To preserve data provenance, the verbatim text from the primary literature was extracted before any harmonisation was applied. Data were extracted into the template set out in the protocol, with linked sheets for studies, small mammal sampling, pathogen assays and sequences (Simons et al. 2025). Of the 728 papers from which data were extracted, 26 were extracted by two team members. D.S. compared the two extractions of each of these papers and kept the more complete one; the choice is recorded in the processing scripts, and the other extraction is not part of the release. In a deviation from the registered protocol, AI tools (Claude Code, Opus 5.5, Anthropic) were used prior to finalisation of database: to find candidate cases of the same field data published in more than one paper, to check extracted records against their source papers and propose corrections, and to check coordinates that fell outside their stated country against the source papers. D.S. decided every cross-study duplicate action and every coordinate that was kept outside its stated country. The individual field corrections were not all reviewed by the authors; their accuracy was estimated from a random sample (see Technical Validation). The release also departs from the protocol in three other ways. The protocol planned to impute non-detections for species detected elsewhere in a study; this was not done, and non-detection records come only from what the papers report, recorded at extraction (see Trapping Effort). The protocol planned to give the uncertainty of each coordinate as a radius; the release gives a categorical coordinate resolution instead (see Technical Validation). Finally, the protocol planned to re-run the search once extraction was complete; it has not been re-run for this release (see Limitations). 3.2 Data Processing and Harmonisation Pipeline To transform the fragmented, verbatim extractions into a relational, machine-readable database, a sequential programmatic pipeline was developed in R (R Core Team 2023). This ensures reproducibility from raw data ingestion to the final database release. The pipeline comprises seven sequential phases: 3.2.1 Corrections to Extracted Records The extraction sheets are not edited after extraction. Corrections are listed in tables in the repository, each with its source in the paper: 3,243 corrections to individual values, 331 deleted rows and 316 re-extracted rows. The pipeline downloads the sheets and applies the corrections to the downloaded copy. It stops if a value in a sheet no longer matches the value a correction expects, so a correction cannot silently overwrite a later change. 3.2.2 Metadata Consolidation Raw extractions are aggregated to consolidate citation metadata and establish unique identifiers for all studies, hosts, pathogens, and sequences. Because historical literature reports temporal data in highly variable formats (e.g., specific days, month-year, multi-year spans), a parsing function was developed to translate verbatim event dates into standardised start_date and end_date bounds, generating a consistent temporal_resolution flag for every record. 3.2.3 Taxonomic and Spatial Resolution Host taxonomy is resolved via the taxize package (Chamberlain et al. 2020), querying the GBIF API to append standardised hierarchies (Species through Class) and persistent taxonID keys (Chamberlain et al. 2026). Concurrently, geographical point data undergo validation against standard administrative boundaries. Coordinates are matched to their corresponding ISO-3166 country codes, and a spatial join against the Database of Global Administrative Areas (GADM, version 4.1) enriches each record with standardised sub- national administrative levels (adm1, adm2, adm3) relevant to the level of geographic resolution (Database of Global Administrative Areas 2022; Hijmans et al. 2024). Where a paper gave no coordinates, the named locality (a village, town or administrative unit) was located using Google Maps, Wikipedia, OpenStreetMap or the GEOnet Names Server, and coordinate_resolution_processed records the level of that locality. One study gives its sites only as GADM version 2.8 municipality identifiers (Wang et al. 2023); these records are placed at a point inside each municipality. 3.2.4 Trapping Effort To support downstream macro-ecological modelling, unstructured, free-text trapping descriptions are parsed to extract trap-night metrics, recorded in trap_nights_clean and described by trap_nights_status. Where source manuscripts reported data in tabular form listing multiple species and sampling sites, zero-detection records were extracted directly from blank or absent cells, preserving the structure of the original study design. Users should be aware that a zero-detection record in host_occurrences reflects a recorded absence within a specific sample, and should not be interpreted as ecological absence from the broader study area. 3.2.5 Pathogen and Genomic Enrichment Pathogen nomenclature undergoes parallel harmonisation against the NCBI Taxonomy database (Schoch et al. 2020). To bridge the gap between ecological sampling and molecular epidemiology, raw NCBI GenBank accession numbers extracted from the literature are passed back through the NCBI Entrez API (Sayers et al. 2024). This automated sequence enrichment downloads and parses the metadata for each accession. The host and pathogen names in each GenBank record are then compared with the names assigned in ArHa, and the differences are listed in the quality assurance report. Differences are not corrected automatically, because GenBank host metadata are often incomplete or give a synonym, an older name or a higher taxon (see Technical Validation). 3.2.6 Cross-study Duplicate Resolution Some field data were published in more than one paper and so entered ArHa more than once. After enrichment, the pipeline resolves these cases from a table of decisions in the processing scripts. Records are removed where a paper repeats data already extracted from another, merged where two papers report complementary results for the same animals, and linked as a duplicate group where the same animals are reported at different spatial or temporal breakdowns that cannot be reconciled (duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events). How the duplicates were found, and how many, is described below. 3.2.7 Quality Assurance and Schema Formatting Prior to final compilation, the pipeline generates a quality assurance report to evaluate database dimensions, coordinate validity, and taxonomic consistency. The final output is then structured into the four-tier relational schema. 3.3 Duplicate Publication of Field Data The same field data may be published more than once: a survey reported in several papers, a synthesis that consolidates earlier studies, or results reanalysed in a later paper. Where a paper does not say that its data have been published before, extraction can duplicate data. The same animals, sites and assay results then enter the database more than once, affecting subsequent counts, prevalences and ranges drawn from, in ways that cannot be seen in the data. To find such cases, each assay record was given a fingerprint of host species, pathogen, number positive, number tested and country, and pairs of studies that shared these fingerprints with overlapping sampling dates were flagged; study totals were compared in the same way. Each flagged pair was checked against both papers. Of the 44 pairs checked, 19 shared counts by chance. The rest were resolved by pre-defined rules: keep the most complete source data; where two papers report the same animals at breakdowns that cannot be merged, keep both and link them; and do not treat a review, or a second copy of the same paper, as a source. In all, 15 studies were removed entirely. Of these, 5 were one paper entered under two citation records. A further 124 host records were removed where two papers overlapped in part, and 43 host records were merged where two papers reported different assays on the same animals. Studies reporting the same animals in formats that cannot be merged are retained and linked through duplicate_group and duplicate_role in sampling_events: 6 studies in 3 groups (see Usage Notes). Each action is listed in the processing scripts and summarised in duplicate_resolution.csv. 3.4 The ArHa Database Explorer To visualise the relational data architecture and improve accessibility for the wider ecological and public health communities, the database is accompanied by the ArHa Database Explorer (https://diddrog11.shinyapps.io/arenavirus_hantavirus_app/). Users can spatially visualise genomic sampling via the Leaflet integration, cross-filter by diagnostic modality or host taxonomy, and export subsets of the data for local modelling. 3.5 Data Records The ArHa database is released under a dual-format strategy to maximise utility and interoperability. Each point is a distinct coordinate; a coordinate used at more than one resolution is shown at its most precise. The numbers in the legend are localities. Figure 2: Contents of ArHa. Host occurrence records tend not to be individual animals. Each record gives the number of animals of one taxon recorded in one sampling session at one locality, and 14,333 records (26.3%) record that a taxon was not caught (individualCount = 0). Records are also unevenly spread across studies: the three studies with the most records, two long- term population studies and one survey of many localities, hold 52% of host_occurrences (Mariën et al. 2020; Cuypers et al. 2023; Guzzetta et al. 2017). Cuypers et al. (2023), for example, sampled 187 localities in Tanzania and reported results for 54 small mammal taxa at each, contributing 10,120 records (18.6% of host_occurrences) from 1,224 animals. Most of these records document that a taxon was not caught at a locality rather than a capture. Analyses that treat records as equivalent units, without reference to individualCount, will therefore over-weight studies of this kind relative to those that report only captures. 3.5.1 Schema Definition A primary vulnerability when archiving complex ecological sampling in flat-file formats is data expansion: forcing many-to-many relationships (e.g., multiple diagnostic assays or genetic sequences derived from a single host) into a single two-dimensional table can result in substantial record duplication. To mitigate this and ensure data integrity, the ArHa dataset is engineered as a four-tier relational database, summarised in Table 1 and Figure 3. Figure 3: The four relational tables of ArHa, their roles in the Darwin Core Archive, their keys and the number of records. Arrows run from the referenced table to the table that holds the key. analysis.background: Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals.
analysis.main_directions: ArHa addresses fragmented surveillance data by standardising host and pathogen taxonomies, resolving duplicate records, and classifying spatial and temporal precision to enable bias‑aware spatial epidemiology.
analysis.current_state: The database compiles 123,101 host occurrence and diagnostic records from a systematic review, structured as a four‑tier relational schema to preserve complex study designs.
analysis.gaps: Data remain limited by variable geographic precision and shifting host nomenclature, and the database relies on published records, potentially underrepresenting unsampled regions.
analysis.future_research: Future work should integrate ArHa with genomic surveillance, refine spatial resolution through georeferencing, and apply the dataset to predictive spillover modelling and policy‑guided surveillance prioritisation.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Arenaviruses and hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens primarily hosted by small mammals. Main directions: ArHa standardises taxonomies, resolves duplicates, and classifies spatial/temporal precision to support bias‑aware spatial epidemiology. Current state: The database compiles 123,101 host occurrence and diagnostic records in a four‑tier relational schema. Gaps: Variable geographic precision, shifting host nomenclature, and reliance on published data limit coverage. Future research: Integrate with genomic surveillance, refine georeferencing, and use the dataset for predictive spillover modelling and surveillance prioritisation.

papers.title: Rational Design of Candidate Hantavirus Gc Fusion Inhibitors Through Structure-Activity Relationship Analysis
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. The viral glycoprotein Gc drives host cell entry through an effectively irreversible prefusion to postfusion transition, making the prefusion state a target for small molecule stabilization. A binding site was defined by comparing the prefusion (PDB 5LJY) and postfusion (PDB 5LJZ) conformations. analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, for which no targeted antiviral therapy exists. (A1)
analysis.methods: The viral Gc prefusion structure (PDB 5LJY) was compared with the post‑fusion structure (PDB 5LJZ) to define a binding pocket bounded by Pro46, Lys310, Asp311, Ile312 and Phe314 (A2, A3, A5). A library of ~3 million compounds was filtered to 1,041 docking‑ready ligands and docked to prefusion Gc (mean predicted affinity –5.35 kcal/mol) (A6). Two parent scaffolds were expanded to 38 analogues (A7) and each analogue was redocked 10 times, evaluated by DBSCAN pose clustering, Gaussian residue‑contact fingerprint, ensemble pose‑drift index, and MM/GBSA rescoring after short relaxation (A9, A10). Rankings were based on weighted residue‑contact score, MM/GBSA, and drift (A11).
analysis.results: The virtual screen produced a mean predicted affinity of –5.35 kcal/mol (A6); analogue SAR‑v17 ranked first by residue‑contact score, ninth by MM/GBSA (–11.08 kcal/mol), and fifteenth by drift (0.094 Å) (A11).
analysis.contribution: The study delivers a structure‑based pipeline and SAR insights for designing small‑molecule stabilizers of the hantavirus Gc prefusion state, generating candidate fusion‑inhibitor molecules for future testing. (A14, A15)
analysis.limitations: All findings are computational predictions; no binding, fusion‑inhibition, or antiviral assays were performed, and only an abstract is available, limiting experimental validation. (A14, A15, evidence_scope)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe disease and lack targeted antivirals (A1). Methods: Prefusion Gc pocket was defined by structural comparison, a ~3M‑compound library was filtered to 1,041 ligands, docked, and 38 analogues were evaluated with clustering, residue‑contact, drift, and MM/GBSA metrics (A2‑A11). Results: Mean predicted affinity was –5.35 kcal/mol; analogue SAR‑v17 ranked first by contact score, ninth by MM/GBSA (–11.08 kcal/mol), and fifteenth by drift (0.094 Å) (A6, A11). Contribution: Provides a computational pipeline and SAR data for candidate hantavirus Gc fusion inhibitors (A14, A15). Limitations: Findings are predictions only; no experimental validation was performed and only an abstract is available (A14, A15).

papers.title: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness.

INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. Despite growing research on hantavirus epidemiology, reservoir ecology, occupational exposure, and diagnostic techniques, important gaps remain in the integration of clinical laboratory preparedness and biosafety within hantavirus response systems [12]. Current international guidance emphasizes that laboratory confirmation requires appropriate serological or molecular testing, while potentially infectious specimens must be handled, packaged, transported, and processed under risk-appropriate containment conditions [1]. However, preparedness also depends on trained personnel, quality-management systems, validated procedures, referral networks, and sufficient resources. A recent Asia-Pacific assessment involving substantial participation from Philippine laboratories identified staff-training and budget limitations among the major barriers to strengthening laboratory quality and competence, indicating broader system-level constraints that may also affect preparedness for uncommon emerging pathogens [19]. These limitations are particularly relevant to hantavirus preparedness in the Philippines. In June 2026, the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine issued specific instructions for the collection, handling, packaging, transport, and referral of specimens from suspected hantavirus cases, emphasizing personnel safety, specimen integrity, coordination with designated reference laboratories, and compliance with biosafety and biosecurity standards [18]. Nevertheless, the existence of national referral guidance does not necessarily indicate that hantavirus testing and biosafety procedures are routinely implemented across hospital and clinical laboratories. Thus, limited evidence regarding decentralized diagnostic capacity, laboratory personnel competency, quality assurance, containment practices, and functional referral pathways represents an important knowledge gap. Systematically evaluating these areas is necessary to determine how effectively Philippine laboratories could recognize suspected hantavirus infections and safely manage and refer to associated clinical specimens, while drawing lessons from laboratory systems in other countries. . Therefore, this systematic review aims to evaluate diagnostic preparedness and biosafety measures for hantavirus infections in clinical laboratories, with particular consideration of their applicability to the Philippines. Specifically, it seeks to identify and compare diagnostic methods used for hantavirus detection; assess laboratory preparedness, testing capacity, quality assurance, and specimen-referral systems; evaluate biosafety measures for specimen collection, processing, transport, storage, and disposal; compare practices across countries and resource settings; identify major diagnostic and biosafety gaps; and determine evidence-based strategies that may strengthen hantavirus laboratory preparedness in the Philippines and comparable resource-limited settings. METHODOLOGY 2.1Study Design and Reporting Framework This study employed a systematic review design to identify, evaluate, and synthesize available evidence on hantavirus infection, with particular attention to epidemiology, human exposure, clinical manifestations, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, biosafety, and implications for public health and laboratory preparedness in the Philippines. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [20]. A structured approach was applied to literature identification, screening and eligibility assessment, data extraction, methodological appraisal, and evidence synthesis. The review protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) [39] under registration number CRD420261485094. Given the heterogeneity of the included evidence in terms of study design, geographical setting, study populations, diagnostic approaches, exposure measures, and reported outcomes, a meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Instead, findings were synthesized using a narrative and thematic approach, allowing evidence to be organized and interpreted across the major domains addressed by the review. 2.2 Literature Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify studies relevant to hantavirus infection and its epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, ecological, and public health dimensions. The principal electronic databases searched were PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Supplementary searches were undertaken through manual screening of reference lists and relevant institutional and research repositories. Grey literature and technical documents from recognized public health organizations and national agencies were also considered when they contributed directly to the objectives of the review. Search terms were combined using Boolean operators and included terms related to Hantavirus, Orthohantavirus, human–rodent interaction, zoonotic transmission, occupational exposure, seroprevalence, reservoir surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, and public health. An example of the search strategy was: (Hantavirus or Orthohantavirus) and (occupational exposure or human–rodent interface or zoonotic transmission) and (seroprevalence or reservoir surveillance or public health) Search terms were modified where necessary to accommodate the indexing systems and search functions of individual databases. 2.3 Eligibility Criteria Studies were considered eligible when they provided evidence relevant to hantavirus infection or transmission, including human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical disease, laboratory diagnosis, occupational or environmental risk, rodent reservoirs, ecological or molecular surveillance, outbreaks, biosafety, or public health implications. Eligible evidence included observational studies such as cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies, as well as outbreak investigations, seroepidemiological studies, ecological and molecular surveillance studies, and other relevant primary investigations. Selected authoritative technical and public health documents were considered when they provided information directly relevant to laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, biosafety, or preparedness. Studies were excluded when they were unrelated to the objectives of the review, provided insufficient information for meaningful interpretation, represented duplicate publications, consisted primarily of opinion or editorial material, or could not provide adequate information for eligibility assessment. Duplicate records identified during the search and screening process were retained only once. 2.4 Study Selection and Screening All records retrieved from the literature search were compiled and screened systematically. The initial search identified 304 records. Duplicate records were removed before screening, after which titles and abstracts were evaluated against the predetermined eligibility criteria. Potentially relevant publications were subsequently assessed through full-text review. Studies that did not satisfy the eligibility criteria at the full-text stage were excluded, with the principal reasons for exclusion documented. Following completion of the screening and eligibility assessment, 18 studies met the inclusion criteria and were retained for the final systematic review. The study-selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram showing the progression of records through identification, duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, full-text assessment, exclusion, and final inclusion. 2.5 Data Extraction Relevant information was systematically extracted from each included study using a structured data-extraction approach. Extracted variables included, where applicable, the author and year of publication, country or geographical setting, study design, study population or sample, sample size, hantavirus species or strain, diagnostic or laboratory method, exposure or reservoir characteristics, principal findings, and implications for clinical practice, laboratory diagnosis, surveillance, or public health. Particular attention was given to findings relevant to human exposure, seroprevalence, clinical manifestations, laboratory detection, rodent reservoirs, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental risks, and biosafety or laboratory preparedness. The extracted information was organized to permit comparison across the 18 included studies and formed the basis of Table 1, which summarizes the characteristics of the included evidence. 2.6 Methodological Quality and Risk-of-Bias Assessment The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed with consideration of their respective study designs. The appraisal focused on the clarity of the study objectives, appropriateness of study design and participant or specimen selection, adequacy of sample size and methodology, reliability of diagnostic or laboratory procedures, completeness of outcome reporting, and potential sources of selection, measurement, and reporting bias. Quality assessment was used primarily to determine the strength and reliability of the evidence and to guide interpretation of the findings rather than as the sole basis for study exclusion. papers.title: SARS, H1N1, EBOLA, COVID-19, MPOX, H5N1 AND HANTAVIRUS: IS HUMANITY ENTERING A NEW ERA OF PANDEMIC? IS TÜRKİYE PREPARED FOR THE NEXT GLOBAL OUTBREAK?
papers.abstract: The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases pose persistent challenges to global health security. Outbreaks such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections highlight the need for effective preparedness against emerging infectious threats. The concept of “Disease X” further emphasizes the importance of preparing for unknown pathogens that may cause future epidemics or pandemics. This study aimed to examine major infectious disease outbreaks and assess Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future global outbreaks. A descriptive review design was employed, based on a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports. The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community-based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats.

The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community-based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats.
